chapter: Clubs, publishers, unions and life in Denver
title: Writing songs with lyricist Andy Razaf
summary: Razaf, who wrote Honeysuckle Rose lyrics with Fats Waller, wrote lyrics to Horace's 'Smooth and Soothing Music' in ten minutes as Horace played the melody; sheet music then earned the money.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: Uh-huh. Did you usually work with a lyricist, or did you write lyrics of your own?

No, we would work with different individuals that were very good with lyrics, like Andy Razaf, the late and great Andy Razaf, the guy that wrote the lyrics to (unintelligible) "Honeysuckle Rose" with Fats Walker. And he and Fletcher did a lot of things together, but of course, I had the pleasure of living in Los Angeles, pretty close to Andy Razaf, even before he was confined to a wheelchair. And I wrote a few things, and I used to go over to his house. I would sit down and play the melody note of the things, man, and he could take his pen and just write right along with you, just as he was writing a letter, you know.

I remember one tune called Smooth and Soothing Music. This is the title that he gave a thing that I was fooling around with, and it was a nice little melody. Boy, he wrote 32 bar lyrics in about ten minutes, and it made sense, you know, and it told a little story, you know, and built up to quite a climax. He was a genius. And Fletcher knew quite a few guys that were great songwriters because when he played Chicago and was broadcasting, of course, this is why a lot of -- how

a lot of these guys survived, you know, and, of course, if you could get the lyrics and get your tune on the air, (unintelligible) naturally it popularized the tune, and they would do anything to get those things on, you know. So in those days it was great. That's why I think that there were better tunes written in those days than things that are being written now, you know, with the exception of a few.
Uh-huh. In those days, of course, money was made more from the sale of sheet music than from recordings.
Whereas nowadays, if -- even if you don't ever really publish a song publicly, you can get it recorded and on an album, which most of the groups do, so it's -- it really is a different thing.
There is a different thing, yeah, a difference. (Inaudible).
Did you -- when you worked with, say, Andy or somebody like that, did you normally write the music first and they would put lyrics to it, or vice versa?

Yes, I would come in with a little piano copy, and I'd play it down. He says, 'let me hear this; played through once.' And while I'm playing through, he could see the veins, you know, right away working, you know, and his mind's working -- and (unintelligible). (Laughter) -- fast. Then he says, 'Okay, let's start again from the top, but do it slowly.' And as I played each part, bar, man, he's
When I get through with my 32 bars, he'd throw that over to me. He says, 'Here are the lyrics.' "your"

Right. He was like that. But a lot of them aren't like that. They got to think and try to make certain passages rhyme, you know; not Andy nonending. These guys would have to erase something, see. "No" "Well, we'll try this." but he had a pattern, just like, you know, you do in playing, you know. He would listen at the melody real close, and when you play the bridge, so he would just -- his mind would be there. He was a was a genius.
